analysis.title: China: Macro CIO Tour Takeaways
key_insights: GS hosted its China macro CIO tour in Beijing on November 3. Invited speakers covered fiscal conditions, property, household consumption, exports, the 2027 growth target, AI/tech policy and US-China relations after the US midterms and four Trump-Xi meetings in 2026.

Fiscal tightening is the most important driver of domestic weakness this year, and the speakers see it as persistent rather than a one-off. Tax revenue to GDP fell from 18.4% in 2012 to 12.6% in 2025 after several rounds of tax cuts.

Non-tax revenue, mainly land sales, is unlikely to rise. Net government debt issuance is already large and may not rise much because the top leadership is concerned about leverage. Population aging raises pension and healthcare spending, so the speakers see tax increases as inevitable and structural.
Property and consumption policies are expected to be limited. Politburo language this year shows no desire for a sharp property rebound, only slower declines and containment of financial contagion.

There is no consensus on which consumption measures would be effective and sustainable. Fiscal reform to strengthen the social safety net and income distribution is hard because of central-local government relations and diverging interest groups.
Export value in USD rose over 20% yoy in the first nine months of 2026. The speakers expect growth to slow to around 10% yoy in 2027, with US and EU trade relationships relatively stable.
China may need to manage its large and rising trade surplus. Goods with export growth above 50% yoy may face reduced VAT export rebates.
The speakers believe policymakers have no pre-determined path for USDCNY and will calibrate the pace of RMB appreciation against export strength.

The 2027 growth target is unlikely to be notably below 4.5% because the 'doubling income between 2020 and 2035' objective still matters to the leadership. Government-driven investment is expected to fill the gap left by weak private demand.

Recent fiscal easing should probably boost next Q1's real GDP. This includes the RMB800bn NPBFI disbursed in September/October and the RMB550bn additional local government bond quota announced in October.

The speakers think this year's policy framework transition may have held the PBOC back from broad-based easing. The policy rate is now the overnight reverse repo rate instead of the 7-day rate, and a conventional rate cut is possible next year, especially if the Fed stops hiking and/or starts cutting.
High-tech including AI is about 20% of China's GDP and 40% of GDP growth. The speakers think its contribution to growth may reach 50-60% in coming years.

Policymakers' mindset has tilted toward risk management in AI and tech. Concerns include uncoordinated and wasteful local government investment in the same areas, potential damage to the financial system and infrastructure, and AI-induced job displacement.
The speakers see US-China relations as an uneasy stability. The Trump-Xi meetings in Beijing and Washington DC set a floor, but tensions may rise in 2027 and 2028.

Reasons for rising tension are possible anti-China measures from the US Congress after the midterms, fewer presidential meetings next year, and the January 2028 Taiwan presidential election. A more confident Beijing is expected to keep tensions under control.

sector_views.rationale: Speakers expect high-tech to rise from 40% to 50-60% of China's GDP growth, and the government is determined to promote AI as a new growth engine, though policy is tilting toward risk management.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Down from 18.4% in 2012 after several rounds of tax cuts. Speakers see tax increases as inevitable and structural.
Strong export growth is the main support for the economy while domestic demand is weak.
Speakers expect a deceleration, with stable US and EU trade relations.
Tied to the 'doubling income between 2020 and 2035' objective. Government investment is expected to fill the gap left by private demand.
Disbursed recently and expected to boost next Q1's real GDP.
Announced in October, expected to support next Q1's real GDP.
A conventional rate cut is possible next year, especially if the Fed stops hiking and/or starts cutting.
High-tech contributes about 40% of GDP growth, and the speakers think this may reach 50-60%.

risk_factors: Persistent fiscal tightening weighs on domestic demand.
Limited property and consumption policy support.
A large and rising trade surplus may require measures such as reduced VAT export rebates for goods with export growth above 50% yoy.
Uncoordinated local government investment in high-tech, AI risks to the financial system and infrastructure, and AI-induced job displacement.
Rising US-China tensions in 2027 and 2028 from US Congress measures and the Taiwan election.
geopolitical: Two Trump-Xi meetings so far this year, in Beijing and Washington DC, are seen as having set a floor for US-China relations, with four meetings in 2026 in total.
Anti-China measures may be introduced by the US Congress after the midterm elections.
The two presidents will not be able to meet as many times in 2027 as in 2026.
The Taiwan presidential election in January 2028 could change US-China dynamics.
China-EU trade consultations have recently taken place, and trade ties with the US and EU should be relatively stable after last year's US-China trade war.

tension_points.bull_case: Two Trump-Xi meetings in Beijing and Washington DC set a floor for relations, structural forces should prevent major escalation, and a more confident Beijing is likely to keep tensions under control.
tension_points.bear_case: Tensions may rise in 2027 and 2028 from possible anti-China measures in the US Congress after the midterms, fewer presidential meetings next year, and the January 2028 Taiwan presidential election.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Anti-China measures introduced by the US Congress after the midterm elections, or changes in dynamics around the January 2028 Taiwan presidential election.
